For most cats, regular bathing is not necessary, as cats are highly effective self-groomers [d4][d10][d7]. According to a Texas A&M veterinary expert, "their fastidious grooming behavior makes this a non-necessary task," and VCA Animal Hospital confirms that "most healthy adult cats are fastidious groomers and rarely require a bath" [d4][d10]. The average indoor cat may never need a bath, and bathing can actually strip essential oils from the coat needed for skin health [d2][d7]. However, bathing does become necessary or beneficial in specific circumstances: if a cat gets into something toxic or hazardous on its fur, if it has mobility issues (due to obesity, arthritis, or age) that prevent proper self-grooming, if it has skin conditions requiring medicated baths, or if it is a long-haired breed prone to matting [d5][d8][d9][d11]. Over-bathing carries its own risks, including dry skin, disruption of natural coat oils, and potential emotional trauma that can damage the human-animal bond [d6][d8][d4]. A combination of regular brushing and the cat's own self-grooming is almost always sufficient for maintaining cleanliness under normal circumstances [d15][d11].
